articles.author: freePS
articles.description:
How to Open a PSD File Without Photoshop


A client just sent you a .psd file. You don't have Photoshop, and installing a trial (or worse, hunting for a cracked copy) just to look at one file feels ridiculous.
Good news: you don't need Photoshop to open a PSD. Modern browsers can parse and render PSD files locally. Here's the fastest way I know.
Open a browser-based PSD viewer. I use freePS — it's free and doesn't ask for an account.
Drag & drop your .psd file onto the page. The file is parsed locally in your browser's memory. Nothing is uploaded to a server, which matters if the file contains client work.
Inspect the layers. Every layer shows up in the Layers panel — you can toggle visibility, reorder, check opacity, or export any state as PNG/JPG.
That's it. From drop to viewing layers takes about five seconds.
Viewing is usually enough, but if you need to tweak something — crop, annotate, fix a typo on a text layer — the same tool has a full online editor with brushes, marquee selection, clone stamp, text, and filters. Export back out as PNG (with transparency), JPG, WEBP, or a JSON project file you can re-open later.
Fair question. Tools like freePS are built entirely on client-side JavaScript: the PSD parsing happens in your browser's memory. You can verify it yourself — open your browser's Network tab while using the tool and you'll see no upload traffic. For client deliverables and anything under NDA, that distinction matters.
Honest answer: for heavy CMYK work, advanced smart objects, or complex adjustment-layer stacks, desktop Photoshop (or a pro-grade alternative) is still the right call. But for the everyday "someone sent me a PSD and I just need to see/edit it quickly" case, a browser tool is faster than any install.
Disclosure: I'm involved with freePS. It's free for personal and commercial use — if it saves you a Photoshop install, it did its job.
articles.title: How to Open a PSD File Without Photoshop (Free, Right in Your Browser)

TL;DR: Treat a transcription upload as two separate checks. First, prove that the selected provider currently advertises a usable speech-to-text model. Then send a tiny known-good audio file with a multipart body generated by a library, including a filename, a credible audio MIME type, and the provider's exact file field name. A marketplace moderation pipeline should preserve the original report and make transcription retryable; it should never turn an ambiguous HTTP 400 into a dropped report.
That order matters. A perfectly formed multipart request cannot make an unavailable capability work, while a malformed boundary can make a healthy service look broken. The useful operational rule is discover first, serialize second, enqueue the human-review item either way.
